Privacy Policy

Last updated: 2026-11-06 (DRAFT — pending legal review)

Who we are

AURA is an on-device voice assistant that can see your screen and perform actions for you when you ask it to. It is built and run by one person, Dinesh Kumar C.

No AURA server ever receives your content

There is no AURA-operated server that receives, stores, or processes your voice, screen content, messages, or files. Everything AURA does runs directly on your phone, or is sent directly from your phone to the services listed below, mainly an AI provider YOU choose and configure with YOUR OWN API key ("Bring Your Own Key").

AURA does operate one small backend, on Google Firebase, and it holds no content. It is not anonymous: it holds your Google sign-in, including your email address, and a record of each install: which phone model and Android version it is running on, which AURA version, and when it last ran. It exists so we know which devices a fix has reached and which ones a change would break, and so abuse can be blocked. It is described in full below. Most of it is on by default and you can switch it off, but your sign-in stays until you ask us to delete it.

What AURA processes, and where it goes

  • Voice: if you turn the wake word on, listening for it happens on your phone and that audio is not sent anywhere. With the on-device voice model, your speech is transcribed on your phone too. Without it, AURA uses Android's speech recognizer: on the phone where that is available, otherwise your phone's default speech service, which may send your audio to its maker (often Google). In live conversation mode your audio goes to your AI provider. Spoken replies use the on-device voice or your phone's text-to-speech service.
  • Screen content: while running a task, AURA reads on-screen elements and can take screenshots to decide what to tap or type. Known banking, payment and authenticator apps are blocked. That list cannot cover every app, and you can add your own restricted apps.
  • App inventory: the names and package IDs of all your installed apps are sent to your configured AI provider only when you run "Scan for sensitive apps", to suggest which ones to restrict. You review every suggestion before it takes effect. During a task, the names of apps that match your request can also be sent.
  • Notifications & media (only if you grant access): read to answer questions and perform actions you request. Notifications from known banking and security apps are filtered out before they reach any AI.
  • Contacts (only if you grant access): matched ON-DEVICE when you say "message <name>", and your contact list is never uploaded. The names and numbers of the contacts that match are sent to the AI doing the task, so it can fill in the call or message.
  • Memory: what AURA remembers about you, and what it learns about apps, is stored encrypted on your phone, with obvious personal details removed on a best-effort basis. The relevant parts are sent to your AI provider during a task.
  • Web research: to learn how a task is done on your phone, AURA may search the web (Google, or DuckDuckGo or Bing) in a hidden browser with a short "how do I…" question, and read the official help pages it finds. The question contains the task in general terms, your phone model, Android version, and the app's name and version. Quoted text and personal details (names, numbers, addresses, message text) are removed before it is sent, and screen content never is. The sites involved see your IP address, as they would for any visit.
  • Web search (only if you add a Tavily key): search queries written by the AI go to Tavily. They can include details from your request.
  • Computers you pair (only if you use the MCP server): they reach the phone directly over your local network (the same Wi-Fi, or a private VPN you set up), encrypted end to end. Nothing about that connection passes through any AURA server. A paired computer receives what its tools return, including screen content, notifications and contact matches, and so does whatever AI it runs.
  • MCP servers you add (only if you add one): the requests the agent makes to that server go straight to it, along with the token you gave it.
  • Voice model downloads (only if you choose them): the files come from Hugging Face, which sees your IP address.

Apart from the services named above, voice, screen content and app names go ONLY to the AI provider (e.g. Google Gemini, Groq, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, or a custom endpoint) that YOU configured with YOUR OWN key, and only while carrying out something you asked for. None of it is copied to any AURA server.

On your phone, AURA keeps session logs of what each task did, including the tool calls, the screenshots taken and what was sent to the AI, for 30 days by default. You can change that or delete them. They stay on your phone unless you choose to share them.

Third-party AI providers — your key, their responsibility

Entering an API key creates a DIRECT relationship between your device and that provider; AURA is not a party to it. That provider's own privacy policy and terms govern what they do with anything you send them (retention, training use, regional storage, etc.), and AURA has no visibility into or control over their practices. Choose your provider carefully and review their policy before use. AURA is not responsible for a third-party provider's handling of your data — that risk sits between you and the provider you selected, not with AURA.

Keys & secrets

Provider API keys you enter are stored in Android's encrypted, on-device preferences (EncryptedSharedPreferences) and are sent only to the provider you configured — never to AURA or anyone else. If a phone's encrypted storage fails, AURA falls back to private app storage that is not encrypted.

Diagnostics — the complete list

AURA uses Firebase Crashlytics and Analytics for crashes and feature usage, and records one row per install so we can see the fleet. These are on by default. Together they collect, exhaustively:

  • the Google account email you sign in with, and the name you told AURA to call you. AURA requires you to sign in with Google; the email is how an install is tied to a real person, and it is the only thing here that is directly about you rather than about your phone.
  • a random per-install ID that resets when you uninstall
  • a one-way hash of your device's Android ID — never the ID itself. It is the only device identifier here that survives reinstalling AURA, and it exists for one reason: so a device that abuses AURA can be blocked and cannot simply reinstall or sign in with another account to get back in. It is salted so it cannot be matched against any other app's view of your device.
  • phone make, model and Android version
  • AURA's version, and whether it is a debug or release build
  • your language and time zone
  • when AURA was installed, how many times the app has been launched, and when it last ran
  • usage counts: how AURA was opened (app, wake word, volume keys, assist gesture); for each task, whether it finished, failed or was cancelled, how many steps it took, how many tool calls failed, a rough duration (such as "10-30s"), a failure category (such as "network" or "rate limit"), and which built-in AI provider ran it ("custom" for one you added)
  • computer connections: the computer's operating system type, a rough session length and how many tool calls it made; pairings approved or refused
  • which onboarding step you reached
  • crash stack traces, and per-tool metrics (which tool ran, how long it took, whether it succeeded)
  • what Google Analytics adds by itself: standard events such as first open and session start, and a rough location (such as country or city) it works out from your IP address. Firebase services see your IP address, as any server does.

That is everything. Never your task content, screen content, tool arguments, tool results, messages, contacts, files, or precise location. AURA asks Google only for your identity — never for access to Gmail, Drive, Calendar or your contacts. There is no advertising ID, no IMEI, no serial number, and no ID that tracks you across other apps. The device hash above is the one device identifier that survives a reinstall, and it is useless outside AURA.

Turn it off with Settings → Privacy & Data → "Share diagnostics". That stops the install row, Analytics and crash reports. Three things keep running either way:

  • Your sign-in: Firebase Authentication keeps your Google account's email, name and profile photo link, which is what signing in means.
  • A block check: about once a day AURA asks our backend whether this device or account has been blocked. It sends the device hash above, a hash of your account ID, and the account ID itself to read your own row, and records nothing.
  • A settings check: at most every 15 minutes AURA fetches shutdown, minimum version and update notices from Firebase Remote Config, which sends a Firebase installation ID, AURA's version and standard request details such as language, time zone and Android version.

How long we keep it

Install rows and sign-ins stay until you ask us to delete them, and the hash of a blocked device or account stays on the blocklist. Analytics and crash data are kept for the periods set in Firebase. To get a copy of your row, or to have it and your sign-in deleted, email us — the app deliberately cannot delete rows itself, because an app that could delete them could also be made to delete someone else's.

What we publish

The website's download page shows totals worked out from those rows: how many phones run AURA and how many are in each country, judged from time zone or language. It publishes only totals, never anything about one install, though a country's total can be as low as one.

Data we sell

None. AURA does not sell your data, and never will.

Your controls

Revoke any permission in Android Settings at any time. Clear stored memory, learnings and activity logs from within the app. Remove a provider key at any time to stop that provider from receiving anything further.

This website

The AURA website uses Vercel Web Analytics to count page visits. Its fonts load from Google Fonts, and its home and download pages ask GitHub for the latest release and download numbers, so those services see your IP address.

Terms of Service

Last updated: 2026-11-06 (DRAFT — pending legal review)

Acceptable use

Use AURA only for lawful purposes and only to automate things you are allowed to do on your own device and accounts. Do not use AURA to bypass security controls or to access accounts that are not yours.

Google sign-in

AURA requires you to sign in with a Google account during setup. The privacy policy says what is kept and how to have it deleted.

You bring your own AI provider

AURA requires you to configure your own API key with a third-party AI provider (e.g. Google Gemini). That provider's terms of service and privacy policy apply to everything they receive from your device through AURA, in addition to these terms. You are solely responsible for choosing a provider, complying with their terms, and any cost, quota, or data-handling consequences of that choice. AURA has no relationship with, and exercises no control over, your chosen provider.

AI can make mistakes

AURA is powered by AI and can misunderstand instructions or act incorrectly. Always review important or irreversible actions. Sensitive actions ask for your confirmation before proceeding, and known banking and payment apps are blocked by AURA's own safety rules. Those rules are not an operating-system guarantee and cannot cover every app.

Blocking and required updates

The developer can block a device or account that abuses AURA, stop AURA for everyone, or require an update before it keeps working. While any of these applies, AURA will not run.

No warranty, limitation of liability

AURA is provided "AS IS", without warranties of any kind, express or implied. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the developer is not liable for any direct, indirect, incidental, or consequential damages arising from your use of the app, from any action AURA takes on your instruction, or from any third-party AI provider's handling of data you sent them. You use AURA, and any provider you configure, entirely at your own risk.

Changes

These terms may be updated; continued use after an update means you accept the new version.
